plan.strategy: Establish a measured baseline with a flat 1D output-tile bilinear kernel that reads the four neighbours through the real input strides and stores one contiguous vector
plan.code_changes: Replaced the seed's 2D broadcast + nested N/C loop kernel (which hard-coded contiguous NCHW addressing and divided by (OH-1) inside a tl.where) with a single flat-index kernel: offs -> (ow, oh, nc) with N/C/IH/IW/OH/OW/ALIGN_CORNERS as constexpr, Python-level branches for the OH==1/OW==1 cases, PyTorch association order for the interpolation, and BLOCK chosen from the flat element count
plan.hypothesis: The parent kernel is ~8500 us on a 262144-element output because of per-program serial N/C loops, runtime modulo and non-contiguous addressing; a flat contiguous-store kernel with constexpr geometry should restore normal vectorised throughput and also make the 1x1 output cases compile

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing the serial N/C loop and runtime index math leaves one contiguous vector store and four gather loads per output element

conclusion.root_cause: All 24 workloads are numerically correct (max abs err 1.95e-3 on bf16, 3.9e-6 on fp32) but the kernel costs ~37.8 ns per output element, exactly linear in element count and identical for fp16/bf16/fp32 -> the cost is per-lane addressing, not bandwidth. The four tl.load calls use vector-of-pointers addresses derived from div/mod chains, so they lower to per-lane non-affine loads instead of block transfers. A target probe showed contiguous block load+store of 8.4M elements takes ~0.03 ms net while the same element count with 4 non-affine loads takes 9.9 ms, i.e. a ~300x penalty for the gather path.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Baseline: geo_mean 0.00163, worst workload timing-1 (0.00071x, 290 ms vs 0.207 ms reference). Device probe evidence: (1) contiguous copy of the timing-1 volume is ~0.03 ms net, so memory is not the limit; (2) per-program overhead on this part is ~37 ns, so program counts in the tens of thousands are themselves expensive; (3) a 2-D tile whose row base is a data-dependent vector but whose last dimension is contiguous (ptr + h0[:,None]*IW + arange(IW)) runs 4.2M elements in 0.188 ms, i.e. the backend handles row-gather with a contiguous minor dimension well; (4) UB register gathers measured at least 9x cheaper than global gather. Conclusion: replace per-lane global gathers with (a) contiguous minor-dimension loads and (b) either an affine expansion for exact integer upscale factors or a UB gather.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Rewrite as a row-tiled kernel: BR output rows per program, contiguous (BR, IW) input row loads with a data-dependent row base, vertical combine, then horizontal resample with no global gather. For the general case use tl.gather on the register tile; for exact integer horizontal upscale factors (OW = 2*IW, as in every timing workload) use a fully affine expansion: load the row shifted by -1/0/+1, build the two interleaved weight branches and select on a length-S constexpr axis so the store stays contiguous. Keep the current flat gather kernel as the correct general fallback.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A modulo-based 'gather' probe is only a real gather if the period does not divide the block size: with BLK=1024 and IWP=4096 the index stayed contiguous inside each block, so the first probe badly under-estimated the gather cost and had to be discarded. Always check that a synthetic irregular-index probe actually destroys affine structure.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 targeted correctness first (all 24 pass, including the 1x1 outputs that previously failed to compile) and used the measurement to falsify 'bandwidth-bound' in favour of 'per-lane addressing bound'.

points.method: 错位全局读取改为片上 gather

plan.strategy: Delete the +-1-element global row loads from the integer-upscale fast path and synthesise the horizontal neighbours with a UB register gather
plan.code_changes: Replaced the two misaligned row-load pairs (ptr_i + rr + ka -+ 1) with two tl.gather calls on the vertically blended row tile, using clamped index vectors (max(k-1,0), min(k+1,IW-1)) so the PyTorch i1p edge rule is still reproduced; removed the now-redundant edge tl.where. Kept the aligned row loads, the affine 2-tap expansion, tl.join and the contiguous 3-D store.
plan.hypothesis: The fast path's 2.5 ns/output is entirely caused by the four +-1-element row loads, which the Ascend backend cannot lower to block transfers (measured 25x penalty vs an aligned base, independent of the offset size). A UB register gather was measured at ~0.1 ms for the same 8.4M lanes, so replacing the shifted loads with tl.gather should cut the kernel cost roughly 30x.

expected_effect.mechanism: Eliminating four misaligned global loads per tile; measured on-target at 21.3 ms -> 0.69 ms for the 8.4M-output geometry, so the geo_mean should rise by roughly one order of magnitude

key_params.rows_per_program: min(2048//IWP, cdiv(n_rows,256)) rounded down, divisor of n_rows

knowledge_uses.application_note: Applied the index/sampling guidance that a scatter or gather must be reorganised rather than tiled blindly: instead of enlarging BLOCK to hide the per-lane cost, the misaligned global access is removed and replaced with a register-level gather.

conclusion.root_cause: The +-1-element row loads were the entire remaining cost and are now removed: they cost 21.3 ms on the 8.4M-output geometry because an Ascend block load needs an aligned base, and the penalty was identical for offsets 1, 2, 8 and 16 elements (~5 ms per misaligned load pair). Replacing them with two clamps plus tl.gather dropped the same geometry to 0.629 ms. All 24 workloads remain numerically correct with the gather-clamped i1p edge rule. The residual gap has two distinct causes: a 0.293 ms 3-D store offset tensor (~10x a flat contiguous store) on the large fixtures, and a ~0.12 ms shape-independent per-call cost that dominates the small fixtures.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected a ~30x drop from removing the misaligned loads; observed 21.3x on the large geometry (0.694 probe vs 0.629 measured, so the probe was accurate) and 186x on the aggregate geo_mean because round 1 was dominated by an even slower path. The frozen target of 0.8x is still missed by 2.6x. Workload-level: large fixtures 0.327/0.425/0.350 (0.629/0.631/0.626 ms) and small fixtures 0.246/0.273/0.238 (0.138/0.138/0.146 ms). The small fixtures are 32x less data but only 4.5x faster, which proves a ~0.12 ms per-call cost independent of shape, exactly where the reference spends its entire 0.034 ms. The large fixtures are still 12x above the measured contiguous-copy floor (0.03 ms net), and the ablation attributed 0.29 ms of that to the 3-D store offsets and the remainder to row-base loads plus gathers.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the two costs the ablation separated: (1) the 3-D (BR,IWP,2) store offset tensor costs 0.293 ms for 8.4M outputs (~10x a flat contiguous store), so build the value tile so the store becomes one flat contiguous block; (2) the small fixtures are now dominated by ~0.12 ms of per-call cost that is not device work (t0 is 0.138 ms while 1/32 of t1's 0.63 ms device time), so measure the fixed launch/wrapper overhead and cut it with a cheaper host path.
conclusion.debug_lesson: An ablation grid over the *number and offset* of loads (2 aligned / 6 with +-1 / 2 aligned+2 gathers / store-only) localised the cost in one pass; the earlier synthetic 'gather' probe had been invalid because its modulo period divided the block size, so it never destroyed affine structure. Verify that a synthetic irregular probe actually breaks contiguity before trusting it.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 established correctness and measured the global per-lane access cost. Round 2 removed it with a register gather, moving the bottleneck to the store path (large fixtures) and to per-call overhead (small fixtures).

knowledge_assessments.rationale: The guidance to reorganise the access pattern instead of enlarging the tile was correct in direction and produced the 186x gain, but the specific replacement it suggests (register/UB gather) is only cheap relative to global per-lane loads; the measured 0.1 ms per 8.4M gather lanes plus the 0.29 ms for the store path show the remaining cost has moved to other constructs, so the guidance is confirmed only for the global-access part.

plan.strategy: Move all metadata-derived launch preparation out of the per-call path with a shape/stride/dtype-keyed scalar cache
plan.code_changes: Added a metadata-keyed cache (key = shape, strides, dtype, output_size, align_corners, scales_h, scales_w) that stores only pre-resolved scalars (grid, rh/rw, constexprs, block/BR) and performs the launch with a literal kernel[grid](...) call in run(); removed the per-call asserts and the per-call parameter derivation. Kernels are unchanged from round 2.
plan.hypothesis: The small timing fixtures are not device-bound: t0 is 0.138 ms while the same kernel shape takes ~0.012 ms of device time, a bare Triton launch costs 0.057 ms and torch.empty 0.010 ms, leaving ~0.06 ms of pure wrapper Python. Caching the metadata-derived launch parameters should remove most of that, helping every workload and the small ones most.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing ~0.06 ms of per-call Python parameter derivation, which is a fixed cost and therefore matters most for the three small timing fixtures

source_ref.locator: section '启动路径与采集兼容性', paragraph on caching compiled artifacts and shape configs

knowledge_uses.application_note: Applied the explicit guidance that compiled artifacts and shape configurations may be cached while the per-call data pointer, stream and tensor metadata must be re-read; the cache stores only scalars keyed on shape/strides/dtype and never a tensor or data pointer.

profile.summary: mixed: Per-program fixed cost dominates device scaling: 512-element programs cost 3.23 us/program while 2048-element programs cost only 6.15 us/program, Large fixture is device-bound and vector-pipeline dominated; contiguous stores are cheap and the row-gather loads are secondary, Small fixtures still spend more than half of eval latency outside the device kernel, even though the kernel itself is also inefficient

conclusion.root_cause: The small fixtures were paying ~0.06 ms of per-call Python for metadata-derived launch preparation (parameter derivation, next_power_of_2, the divisibility loop, kwarg binding). Caching the resolved scalars keyed on shape/strides/dtype/output_size/options removed about two thirds of it. All 24 workloads still pass with unchanged numerics, and the cache holds no tensors, storage or data pointers, re-deriving an entry whenever shape, strides or dtype change.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected ~0.06 ms of per-call Python with the small fixtures recovering most of it; observed exactly that: t0 0.1385 -> 0.1013 ms, t2 0.1375 -> 0.1047, t4 0.1460 -> 0.1024, i.e. a 0.036-0.044 ms saving per call, lifting the geo_mean from 0.3033 to 0.3450. The remaining per-call floor is now ~0.09 ms (0.057 ms Triton launch + 0.010 ms allocation + ~0.012 ms device time), which is already 2.6x the reference's entire 0.030-0.040 ms for these shapes, so the small fixtures are close to their structural limit under a Triton launch. The large fixtures did not move (0.629/0.632/0.626 ms) because they are device-bound, not host-bound, confirming the round-2 conclusion that their cost is split roughly evenly between the row-base loads and the 2x-size store path.
conclusion.next_suggestion: The three large fixtures are device-bound at 0.63 ms for 8.4M outputs and were unchanged by this round, so the last round should target the kernel: the load and store masks (including the `other` select) are still applied on every access even when n_rows is divisible by BR and IWP == IW, and the store mask costs a select over a tile twice the size of the value tile. Elide both with a constexpr FULL flag for the provably in-range case.
conclusion.debug_lesson: For a launch-overhead probe, time a kernel-only loop and a bare empty-kernel loop too: the difference between full run() and the kernel-only loop exposed 0.06 ms of pure wrapper Python that no device metric would have shown. Also, the candidate-admission gate requires a literal kernel[grid](...) in the source, so a cached closure launcher is rejected even though it is functionally identical.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Rounds 1-2 fixed the kernel's memory access pattern (0.0016 -> 0.3033). Round 3 fixed the host path (0.3033 -> 0.3450). Round 4 should return to the kernel for the large fixtures, which the host fix cannot help.

source_ref.locator: section '启动路径与采集兼容性', paragraph on caching compiled artifacts and shape configs

knowledge_assessments.rationale: The guidance that compiled artifacts and shape configurations may be cached while the per-call data pointer and metadata are re-read held exactly: caching only scalars keyed on shape/strides/dtype/out_size/options improved the small fixtures from 0.246/0.273/0.238 to 0.301/0.383/0.296 with identical kernels, and the per-call cost dropped from 0.138 ms to 0.102 ms. No tensor, storage or pointer was cached and the input views were re-derived each call.

plan.strategy: Elide load/store masks and `other` selects with a constexpr flag for the shape where every tile lane is provably in range
plan.code_changes: Added a FULL constexpr to the integer-upscale kernel: when n_rows is divisible by BR and IWP == IW every lane of every tile is provably in range, so both the load mask (with its `other` select) and the store mask over the double-size (BR,IWP,2) tile are omitted. Host computes FULL alongside the other cached launch scalars; kernels otherwise unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The large fixtures are device-bound at ~0.63 ms for 8.4M outputs and pay an always-on mask plus `other` select on every access, including a select over a (BR,IWP,2) tile twice the size of the value tile; dropping them where provably unnecessary should reduce the per-element instruction count and improve those three workloads.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing a per-element predicate and select from the two loads and, more importantly, from the store tile that is twice the value-tile size; this is device work, so it should move the three large timing fixtures that the round-3 host fix could not reach

conclusion.root_cause: The elided predicates were not on the critical path: the constexpr FULL flag removed the load mask, its `other` select, and the store mask over the (BR,IWP,2) tile, yet the large fixtures moved by less than the measurement spread and the small ones regressed slightly. This reproduces the round-2 ablation result (masked 0.5941 ms vs unmasked 0.5944 ms) end to end, so the large-fixture cost is in the data movement itself, not in predicate handling.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected the mask/`other` removal to move the three device-bound large fixtures; observed no change: t1 0.6293 -> 0.6230 ms, t3 0.6316 -> 0.6244, t5 0.6260 -> 0.6174 (inside the run-to-run spread), while the small fixtures moved in both directions (t0 0.1013 -> 0.1130, t2 0.1047 -> 0.1143, t4 0.1024 -> 0.1202). The aggregate geo_mean therefore went 0.3450 -> 0.3442, i.e. no improvement, so round 3 remains the best. The null result is consistent with the round-2 measurement that masks cost essentially nothing, and confirms that the large fixtures are limited by the row-base loads plus the two UB gathers rather than by per-element predicates.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Round 2's own ablation already answered this: masks were free (0.5941 vs 0.5944), so the remaining large-fixture cost is data movement through data-dependent row bases and the two UB gathers, not predicates. Any further work should either (a) make the source-row access fully affine by loading a contiguous input band per program and gathering inside it, or (b) reduce the number of gathers per output element; simply removing more predicates will not help.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Mask and `other`-select elision is not where this kernel's cost lives: the predicates were already cheap relative to the data movement, so a change that looks like an obvious instruction-count win must still be measured rather than assumed. Round 2's ablation had already shown masks are free (k2_center_nomask 0.5944 vs k2_center_masked 0.5941), and this round independently reproduced that null result end to end.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Rounds 1-2 fixed the access pattern (0.0016 -> 0.3033), round 3 fixed the host path (0.3033 -> 0.3450), and round 4 tested the last cheap instruction-level hypothesis and falsified it, so the best candidate remains round 3's.

plan.hypothesis: The large fixtures are device-bound at ~0.63 ms for 8.4M outputs and pay an always-on mask plus `other` select on every access, including a select over a (BR,IWP,2) tile twice the size of the value tile; dropping them where provably unnecessary should reduce the per-element instruction count and improve those three workloads.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing a per-element predicate and select from the two loads and, more importantly, from the store tile that is twice the value-tile size; this is device work, so it should move the three large timing fixtures that the round-3 host fix could not reach

conclusion.root_cause: The elided predicates were not on the critical path: the constexpr FULL flag removed the load mask, its `other` select, and the store mask over the (BR,IWP,2) tile, yet the large fixtures moved by less than the measurement spread and the small ones regressed slightly. This reproduces the round-2 ablation result (masked 0.5941 ms vs unmasked 0.5944 ms) end to end, so the large-fixture cost is in the data movement itself, not in predicate handling.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected the mask/`other` removal to move the three device-bound large fixtures; observed no change: t1 0.6293 -> 0.6230 ms, t3 0.6316 -> 0.6244, t5 0.6260 -> 0.6174 (inside the run-to-run spread), while the small fixtures moved in both directions (t0 0.1013 -> 0.1130, t2 0.1047 -> 0.1143, t4 0.1024 -> 0.1202). The aggregate geo_mean therefore went 0.3450 -> 0.3442, i.e. no improvement, so round 3 remains the best. The null result is consistent with the round-2 measurement that masks cost essentially nothing, and confirms that the large fixtures are limited by the row-base loads plus the two UB gathers rather than by per-element predicates.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Round 2's own ablation already answered this: masks were free (0.5941 vs 0.5944), so the remaining large-fixture cost is data movement through data-dependent row bases and the two UB gathers, not predicates. Any further work should either (a) make the source-row access fully affine by loading a contiguous input band per program and gathering inside it, or (b) reduce the number of gathers per output element; simply removing more predicates will not help.
conclusion.debug_lesson: Mask and `other`-select elision is not where this kernel's cost lives: the predicates were already cheap relative to the data movement, so a change that looks like an obvious instruction-count win must still be measured rather than assumed. Round 2's ablation had already shown masks are free (k2_center_nomask 0.5944 vs k2_center_masked 0.5941), and this round independently reproduced that null result end to end.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Rounds 1-2 fixed the access pattern (0.0016 -> 0.3033), round 3 fixed the host path (0.3033 -> 0.3450), and round 4 tested the last cheap instruction-level hypothesis and falsified it, so the best candidate remains round 3's.

plan.strategy: Replace per-output-row 256-byte row loads with contiguous multi-KB input blocks and reuse one row pair for two output rows, in a single kernel launch
plan.code_changes: Replaced the fast-path kernel with _blk2x_kernel: one program owns QB consecutive input rows of one image and loads two contiguous multi-KB blocks (rows lb..lb+QB-1 and lb+1..lb+QB) instead of two 256-byte row loads per output row; the same row pair yields the even output row and the odd row one position lower, so two mixed tiles cover 2*QB rows. The two clamped end rows are written by an extra (NB+1)-th program per image inside the same launch. Block size QB*IW is capped at 2048 float32 elements, and the new path requires a fully contiguous NCHW input and the exact 2x geometry; everything else keeps the round-2 kernels. The compiled-launcher fast path is kept and moved to the merged kernel.
plan.hypothesis: The large-geometry deficit is caused by per-row 256-byte loads (65536 transfers, 45 GB/s), not by volume or the store. Switching to contiguous input blocks should cut the 0.629-0.630 ms large-geometry latency to roughly a quarter while leaving the small host-bound cases at parity.

expected_effect.mechanism: Multiplying the transfer size per address computation by 2*QB (256 B row fragments -> multi-KB contiguous block transfers) should remove the measured 316 us of load time on the large geometry while keeping the cheap store, cutting large-geometry latency about 2.3x

key_params.policy: QB=min(IH//2, 2048//IW) halved until IH%QB==0 and N*C*(IH//QB)>=128
